text: It's welcome everybody to our council meeting of November 9th. Before we get going and I asked the clerk to start the meeting, I want to take just a few seconds and just speak to our community about the news we received on the weekend. We're all aware now that Algoma Public Health has confirmed eight new COVID cases in our community over the course of the weekend. And I think that really represents a wake up call for all of us. I think Sault Ste. Marie and Algoma did a very good job when this pandemic began in following public health advice. And I think eight months in, it's getting really tough to follow that advice and to continue to stay committed to it. I think naturally and understandably, a lot of us are becoming impatient with how our lives have been adjusted and the sacrifices that we have to make. But during those times, it's more critical than ever that we continue to follow public health advice. We see that the virus is really increasing in number in parts of the world, in parts of Canada, United States and Ontario. And we have no reason to expect that won't continue to happen in our community. If we want to keep our community safe, we wanna keep our kids safe that are in school and our kids safe that are in daycare, our seniors safe, all the folks that we love and wanna take care of that are in our retirement homes, our family and our friends and our community at large, the best way that we can all do that is to keep COVID out of our community and to keep COVID from spreading in our community. And the only way we can do that is if we follow public health advice. So I wanna take the opportunity to ask our community to recommit to Algoma Public Health's advice, to do what you can to follow Algoma Public Health's advice and to encourage the people in your life to follow Algoma Public Health's advice. If you see people who aren't following it, please speak to them kindly and honestly and ask them to follow it. Let's also take the time to have patience with one another and encourage one another through these challenging times. I have a tremendous amount of faith in our community and I'm sure we can get on the right track again, but we have to commit to follow Algoma Public Health's advice. Thank you. speaker: lisacase
text: Good afternoon, everyone. Thank you again for this opportunity to provide an update. We have had a number of conversations with Mayor Provenzano and trying to work with all of our community partners and those that are invested in improving care in our community. My name is Lisa Case. I'm currently the Director of Mental Health and Addictions here at Tsure Hospital. I've been with our hospital since 2001 and started my work as a clinical social worker in Mental Health and Addictions. In 2013, I transitioned into a leadership position within the Mental Health and Addictions program. And then earlier this year moved into the clinical director role. I certainly appreciate the work and the folks that I get to do this work with. In the next slide, you'll see, I think probably what no new news for anyone, but just a little bit of an update on the findings from our chief coroner in Ontario. In 2019, we were up over almost 100 more deaths related to opiates. And then year to date, we're over 25% higher across Ontario. This continues to be an issue throughout North America, throughout Canada, throughout Ontario. If we move to the next slide, you'll see sort of our Northeast Ontario public health findings. And both the concerning areas for me are certainly the emergency department visits. We never want people to have to present to the emergency department unless absolutely necessary. And you'll see that those have skyrocketed since 2016, but also more concerning to me, both personally and professionally would be the number of deaths in Northeast Ontario. And then according to Algoma Public Health last week, we're seeing that even additional losses across Ontario. So we've experienced 26 confirmed opiate related deaths and it's anticipated that by end of year, we could reach between 52 and 60 if the current pace continues. When we look at Northeastern Public Health, we're seeing even higher rates, 105 for the first six months of this year that have lost their lives to opiate related issues compared to a total of 119 in all of 2019. So in the first six months, we're on track to be double. The losses associated with addictions in our community have been encompassing for, I know for staff and physicians and leaders at Surrey Hospital and our collaborative care partners across the community, the impact does hit us both personally and professionally. We are members of this community. But what we'd like to do today is to talk a bit about what we have accomplished as a community and with community partners and where we're headed. And that starts with an update from just a quick review on what council supported back in 2018 in our next slide. Thank you. So really today, we wanna provide an update on where we were and where we are and where we're headed. In 2018, city council passed a resolution of support for the six things that you'll note there. One was to meet the residential withdrawal management standards of care and obtain what we have traditionally called level three withdrawal management. We'll talk about that in a few minutes. The second piece was to provide an outreach program that provided harm reduction strategies and supports treatment engagement. So to catch people before they need extremely intensive care, but also when they do need more intensive care. In the third piece, you'll see that we were asking at that time to expand our safe bed program. At the time we had two beds, we wanted to expand that program to include stabilization and transitional beds. Number four was develop a day evening treatment program that allowed for the right care close to home. We have a great number of folks in our community that have to be transferred out of our community to receive the right level of care. We're working on that. We do have an update on that. Number five was invest in transportation needs for those accessing services, creating more accessible services. And number six was to co-locate the existing and potential new mental health and addiction services in the community for improved coordination of care. If we look at the next slide, we'll see a little bit of where we're at to date. So number one, medically supported withdrawal management, including the rapid access addiction medicine and consultation team. For that number one, the level three withdrawal management terminology is actually being redefined provincially to reflect more of a full continuum of care and the services that encompass addiction care, including care at home. So individuals that can, with the right supports and the right sports medically, as well as psychosocially can do that withdrawal management what would be traditionally called detox. They can do that in the comfort of their own home where they have an appropriate space to do that. When they don't, we have community-based care in a residential withdrawal management or utilization of rapid access addiction medicine through medication. Or when necessary in hospital care. So that sometimes ends up being our ICU, our intensive care unit, or acute medicine floors within our hospital. That entire continuum of care is based on the clinical care needs of that individual and their choice of where they would prefer to receive service. In April, 2018, we were a community that was fortunate enough to have the investment of the Rapid Access Addiction Medicine Clinic along with our Northeastern community partners, Timmins, North Bay, Sudbury as well, all received support for hub sites for that service. And the purpose of the Rapid Access Addiction Medicine is to have a low barrier walk-in service for those individuals that are wanting help or assistance with a substance use disorder. The RAM right now is currently located within our addictions treatment clinic. The clinic itself is staffed by physicians, a registered practical nurse, master's prepared addictions counselors, and administrative support. And to date, so since their opening in April of 2018, they've helped 650 unique individuals that have engaged in care in that community-based service. That to be said, there are still a lot of people that need support in our community and we do work closely with the other medication-assisted treatment services that are offered throughout our community that we do try and address wait times there as well. Additionally, in that same number one, this year we've been able to add registered nursing staff to the model of care provided within our residential withdrawal management. Again, I'll say, historically we've called that detox. The service by, we've added that service to the services that were being provided by our addiction service workers. So those would typically be social service worker trained individuals providing that psychosocial support. The change in care is allowing us to increase our capacity to provide improved and safer care for those with complex addictions and mental health presentations, and allowing the staff to focus on their level of expertise and to focus on therapeutic interactions. Then more recently, along with our partner hospitals across the Northeast, we've been able to introduce addiction medicine consult team. That is a registered nurse and a registered addiction service worker. And that team provides consultation and expert advice across the hospital and to community partners in helping to treat those that are impacted by substance use. Some of that is what we would call motivational interviewing helping improve the person's insight and their readiness to change. And support for substance use withdrawal, maintenance and replacement therapies. That team is in its infancy right now. Those are the teams across the Northeast are learning from each other. They're working very closely together to try and provide the most consistent care possible. We will see that work improve over time. The care that those teams are providing is based solidly in the principles of compassion, social justice and evidence-based treatment. Within our next piece, you'll see the current collaborative planning for mobile mental health and addictions in primary care. This piece I'm pretty excited about. There isn't a piece that I'm not excited about, but this one in particular, we're working with a number of our close community partners across social services, justice, primary care and mental health and addictions. I apologize if I missed anyone, but we're working to launch a mobile community wellness bus. And the primary focus of that service will be to meet clients in the community where they're at both physically and mentally and provide basic levels of care and interventions from a nursing, addictions and mental health and peer worker perspective. That mobile community wellness bus will provide safe and welcoming presence in our community. And particularly right now in our downtown core where people are struggling to access services and overcome those barriers to care. Collectively, if the opportunity presents itself, we would welcome the opportunity to come back to council perhaps next month to provide a more in-depth details of that collaboration and a launch time. Additionally, if we look to number three, we've been able to expand our mental health and justice safe beds from two beds to six beds. And in our 2018 ask, we were thinking nine beds. What we have received in investment thus far has allowed us to move to six beds. That service is currently co-located and has been and will continue to be co-located within our residential withdrawal management. We see a great overlap in the service needs of the individuals accessing that care. Excuse me. So four of these beds, four of the six beds are specifically intended to support those experiencing a mental health or addictions crisis and have immediate or acute police involvement. They are, for example, they're apprehended under the Mental Health Act, brought to hospital for an assessment. They may be assessed and determined that they don't require a hospital admission, but they do require intensive support. And our safe bed program is the appropriate space to be able to do that. The length of stay for that program can be on average 30 days. So it does give people an opportunity to get stable, to get their feet under them, to get connected to the additional adjunct supports that they need. Another piece that I'm quite excited about, and it's in its truly just born today, where we're currently launching a concurrent disorders day treatment program. And that's number four in that areas of improvement that council supported. Based on a needs assessment throughout the Northeast, this type of care was identified as a top priority. We've chosen to work towards launching it without any formal investment, but we know it's necessary and needed in our community. It's specifically designed for individuals that are struggling both with substance use and mental health issues. We do see the prevalence or coexistence of those issues very closely linked together. The program is designed for individuals that are age 16 and over right now, who have been diagnosed with moderate or severe substance use and mental health disorders. And the goal of that day treatment program is to provide again, low barrier access to intensive treatment along the continuum of care with patients that are ready to make some change in their substance use. Our clinical team offers assessment treatment for concurrent disorders that includes psychology, psychiatry, counseling, psychotherapy, and access to addictions medicine. We've been working very closely with Royal Ottawa Hospital, as well as the quality lead for the mental health and addictions table with the Northeast LHIN or Ontario Health North. When we move to number five, we look at the continued efforts are being made for transportation and accessing care. The mobile care that we've referenced before above with the mobile wellness van, I think is an excellent example of working together with our community partners of how we will make, not necessarily make it easier for people to get to the service, but let's bring the service to them wherever possible. But where we have unique services like our residential withdrawal management, what we typically do is work with our community partners, including social services like Ontario Works to get folks access to the bus passes they need. We have single use bus passes, as well as coordinate with case management. And at times our local taxi companies to help people get to the care that they need and support them in that. There have been a few other areas that we've improved upon that weren't part of our mandate back in 2018. We've seen our mobile crisis rapid response team, which was a collaboration with Sault Ste. Marie City Police that we started similar to this concurrent disorder day treatment program is that we started it within our own resources and piloted and we were successful enough that this year we've received some enhanced funding that is now allowing us to go seven days a week, 10 hours a day. We are also working closely with our Anishinaabeg police partners and our OPP partners to see how we can emulate that relationship. So that if you're someone accessing that care or receiving that service or that intervention in Sault Ste. Marie, or perhaps you're north of the city or east of the city, you can have a consistent experience within that care system. So we're working to try and utilize what we've learned and what works well with our Sault Ste. Marie City police partners, with our other police partners as well. Then again, in something else that we had maybe hoped for, but weren't asking for specifically, we received support with our community in December, 2019 peer support in our Surrey Hospital Emergency Department launched. We've had some troubles through the pandemic obviously, but that service has been back in and assisting in the patient or the care experience for a number of months again now. It's a community collaboration that again, is led by Canadian Mental Health, but with eight other community partners that are on board right now to help house needle exchange, addiction medicine, hepatitis C, HIV harm reduction efforts. It's still in its infancy. So we just received word this past summer that we were successful to this. We are actively working together to figure out how we can add to this service and find a permanent location for that service as well. So if we can move on to the next slide, I'll demonstrate a little bit more about where we're going. So you'll see a phased approach outlined in the slide. I think anyone who's been paying attention to social media and that would know that we've had some challenges with our building, the residential withdrawal management was located in down on Queen Street. And as a result of the review of the cumulative and rising risks related to the facility deficiencies, longstanding and increasing infection control risks, perhaps nudged over the line by the pandemic. On March 29th, 2020, the 911 Queen Street location was deemed permanently unviable. The residential withdrawal management and safe bed services have been temporarily relocated to Surrey Hospital and currently remain at the 950 Great Northern Road location. In May of this year, a revised addiction services submission was provided to the Ministry of Health and Ontario Health North, highlighting the urgent need and requesting review and approval of this revised submission. Currently that submission represents the phased approach that you'll see in this slide. Since that time, we've participated in a number of joint meetings with both the Ministry of Health and community partners to help navigate and move this application forward. I say this as seriously as I possibly can, our commitment to that is unwavering. If we looked at the next slide, it outlines phase one in a bit more detail. So the check marks you'll see are things that we already have in motion. So we have our addiction service workers and our registered nurses supporting withdrawal management and our mental health and justice safe beds. And we have four medical beds that are withdrawal management beds within Surrey Hospital. We're currently looking for an appropriate permanent community-based location. We are also looking to increase from five to eight acute admission beds. So at the old site, we had five cots in one tiny room. That wasn't appropriate for probably quite some time. I don't think we'd have anybody that would dispute that. We're also looking at right-sizing from 11 post-acute beds to 10 post-acute beds. And that would include those six mental health and justice safe beds, as well as what we would call two alternative level of care beds. Those are low sensory beds. They might have been using a stimulant like methamphetamine or crystal meth, as it's called. They may have cognitive impairments. Excuse me. And what you'll see right now with the changes in the continuum of care and the progress that we have made, we've been able to reset that model of care to represent a total bed count of 24, with four of those beds, as noted, that are in hospital. The service composition is based on ongoing investments and enhancements over the past two years, best practices, trying to meet the care needs across the continuum, including those that can be cared for safely in their home as outpatients, and then more intensely in a residential or hospital setting. That's that piece we talked about, that if we can get more of the intensive outreach, the assertive outreach, the community-based care, then the research would show that we can help people earlier in the process and not necessarily require a residential stay. But we want to have the right number of beds for those that do need that residential stay. If we move to the next phase, you'll see that we've actually achieved two of the three pieces where we're headed. And it's tentative in the sense that the Concurrent Day Evening Treatment Service is a pilot. At this time, we want to work with and learn from our patient and family advisors that are participating in the development of it, as well as from our regional and provincial partners. So we know that that service will continue to evolve. We have been providing problem gambling, gaming and technology use treatment for many years now. But we are working on enhancing our service, knowing that the challenge becomes when so much of the service has had to move to virtual care in the pandemic and in the response to the pandemic that we're often then asking people to engage in care for perhaps a dependency on technology, and they're having to utilize technology in order to access that care. The piece that is not yet checked, but I feel like I want to check it is the assertive outreach and that mobile harm reduction in healthcare. And that is in progress. This piece in itself includes the formalization and expansion of that day treatment service, as well as those collaborative efforts together as a community and with community partners to provide that local community-based healthcare. If we move to phase three, this is all about the consolidation and sustainability of the program. So when we talk about a permanent appropriate location for residential withdrawal management, we would like to consider the phase two and phase three in that search for an appropriate space. We would propose and have proposed a hub site consolidation of phase one and two, those foundational services, the specialized services, and an enhanced collaborative care model with both the mobile services and the spokes sites throughout to St. Marie and Algoma. What we've seen, we've had some significant success with our rapid access addiction medicine. So the hub currently is located on East Street and we have spoke sites in Wawa with Lady Dunn Hospital, and then as well in East Algoma. And based on what each community's need is, Richards Landing, Thessalon, Bruce Mines, some work that we're doing to build relationship in Elliott Lake, although they have strong addiction services in Elliott Lake now, we're working on how we can enhance that relationship as their needs change, as well as Blind River. So we wanna build upon the model that we know is working, not just in Sioux St. Marie, but across the region and across the province and develop a hub site where to some extent, one-stop shopping for your mental health and addictions needs, but with close ties to both mobile and spoke services. Home-based withdrawal management, I'm optimistic in that, that is a missing piece right now that we want to, anyone that has a safe home-based environment to receive that care, that support, we want them to be able to do that. In the same way that our renal dialysis patients can receive that care in their home when appropriate. Our folks that are struggling with active addiction issues, we want them to have equitable care in that. The next piece that I've talked about a fair bit is that concurrent disorders day evening treatment program. And that's in yellow as well, because we are piloting it. They started today. Our biggest need is that permanent location for the medically supported residential withdrawal management. When we roll up this entire continuum of care, and if we can achieve that here in Sault Ste. Marie and for Algoma, we must continue to be mindful of an individual's journey.
